Interpreted through standard monetary policy research, the FOMC’s message is cautiously positive: in a New Keynesian/Taylor-rule framework, calling the Q1 slowdown “transitory,” emphasizing a symmetric 2 percent inflation goal, holding the funds rate at 0.75–1.00 percent, and maintaining reinvestments via IOER/ON RRP point to gradualism and continued accommodation.

Adjusting with April 2017 SLOOS insights, the credit backdrop is mixed and slightly less supportive than the statement alone implies. Banks reported tighter standards in key areas—particularly CRE (with vacancy-rate and property-price concerns) and auto loans—while foreign banks widened loan-rate spreads and lowered LTVs, indicating some tightening of terms. At the same time, banks eased standards on credit cards and maintained willingness to lend on consumer installment loans. These survey results suggest modest headwinds for business and certain consumer credit channels even as labor markets are solid and business investment has firmed.

Netting the FOMC’s constructive macro tone against SLOOS’s pockets of tightening, the overall stance remains cautiously positive but moderated by credit conditions.
